items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I looked up Johnny Dodds the other day, and there's not one record.

ctx.x: Saying that maybe 6,000 people are really interested in jazz altogether in the country, uh, and, uh, not so many of those are maybe interested in, uh, in the New Orleans style, actually. When you look at the, uh, uh, uh, Swan catalog, say, you'll see maybe, oh, 40 or 50, uh, Miles Davis records, and, uh, let's see, I looked up Johnny Dodds the other day, and there's not one record. This isn't the latest one, this was a year old. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. There wasn't one Johnny Dodds record in the whole place. So you…
Look at all the histories of jazz that come out and barely mention Johnny Dodds. Yeah. If they mention him at all.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: When I talked to Johnny Dodds—we were writing Jazzmen in those days, 1938—and I was asking about the breakup of the Oliver Band.

ctx.x: So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…
Well, of course, we'll never know what Joe Oliver really sounded like.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: Things were really bad and that's about how bad it was there when Johnny Dodds was playing this little trio job. So he invited me to his home next day.

ctx.x: 1949. It says here she was approximately later, 11 years older than George Bakke. I figured that out. To get on to a few other people that I used to talk to, the next one on this list was Johnny Dodds, whose notes I'll have to send. They probably are in a box of Baby Dodds notes, I think. I was always going to try to rewrite them. When I first met Johnny Dodds about 1936, I went to Chicago and I inquired if he was playing anyplace or where he was. All I knew about him, he'd been on some of the jelly roll records…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: I wouldn't have hardly known who he was at that time when Johnny first introduced me.

ctx.x: Now these are typed in the back of the Defender notes.

Yeah. That's some of the later Defender notes, some things that I probably didn't get. He probably looked through my notes and then went up there and went through a couple of years. We'll copy all this stuff for you. So in any case, there are a few other interviews, people that are dead there like Tubby Hall and Joe Lindsay. Unfortunately, we got very little bit from Tubby Hall. I wanted to apologize on that. He was one of the great drummers, I'm convinced the more I hear of other drummers especially. At that…
